title: The boy who never heard "no cakes"
hook: a commentary story: Anuruddha was so rich he didn't know the words "there isn't"; grown up, he learns from his brother that the farm work never ends (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)
tomorrow: Eight thoughts of a great person

segments.voice: Yesterday: vinaya. Upali answered Kassapa's questions until the discipline was recited. Your line was the rules remembered. Today, one of the princes who went forth with him, and a word he had never heard.

A golden bowl, with a lid on it, carried from a mother to her son. The boy is Anuruddha, a Sakyan remembered as a cousin of the Buddha, and the commentaries tell this story about his childhood. He's playing a game with friends, and the stakes are cakes. He loses, and sends a servant home to his mother: send cakes. She does. He loses again, and again. Finally his mother sends word back: there are no cakes. Anuruddha, the story says, has never heard the words there isn't. He assumes it's a new kind of cake, and sends back: then send me some no-cakes.
screen: `A COVERED GOLDEN BOWL.` → `HE LOSES, AND LOSES AGAIN.` → `SEND ME SOME NO-CAKES.`

segments.voice: First, the bowl. In the commentary, his mother decides to teach him what there isn't means, and sends an empty bowl with the lid on. It says devas filled the bowl with heavenly cakes on the way, because of a gift Anuruddha had made in an earlier life. So the boy who had never heard no still doesn't hear it. Second, years later, in the Vinaya. His older brother, Mahanama, says someone from their family ought to go forth, and it should be one of them. Anuruddha says he's too delicate for that life. So Mahanama explains what staying home involves. The fields must be plowed, then sown, watered, drained, weeded, reaped, gathered, threshed. Third, Anuruddha's question: when does the work end? It doesn't, his brother says. Our father and grandfather died with the work still going. Now Anuruddha hears what was underneath every cake: a household's work that never ends. Then you look after the house, he says. I'll go forth. Fourth, here's one way to read the two stories together. Comfort can be exactly this: never hearing there isn't, because someone else hears it for you. His mother heard it. His brother would go on hearing it in the fields. The story doesn't mock the boy. It shows the moment he finally asks where things come from, and the answer turns him toward going forth.
screen: `AN EMPTY BOWL, FILLED ANYWAY.` · `WHAT DOES THE FARM TAKE?` · `WHEN DOES THE WORK END?` · `SOMEONE ELSE HEARS THE NO.` · then, large: `THERE ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Find one thing in your day that came to you without you ever hearing there isn't: hot water, a quiet room, food in the cupboard, a language people understand when you speak. Follow it back, the way Mahanama walked his brother through the fields, and ask who carried it here, who heard no so you didn't have to. No guilt is needed; just see them, for a few breaths.
Natthi, there is not. The words Anuruddha had never heard, until his brother showed him the farm work that never ends. Today's word.
Your line: there isn't. Someone, somewhere, hears the no for you. Day seven hundred forty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Teachers in Theravada communities tell Anuruddha's childhood story with a smile, and the Vinaya's farm conversation is read as a picture of the household work that monastics leave behind and that lay supporters still carry.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funny story about a spoiled boy.
what it means: a boy who never heard "there isn't", because others heard it for him, grows up to ask where the cakes came from.
what a scholar hears: the cake story is commentarial; the conversation with Mahanama about plowing, sowing and threshing is in the Vinaya's Cullavagga, which tells how the Sakyans went forth.

chat.says: Why did hearing about farm work make Anuruddha leave home?
options: He finally saw a household's work never ends, so he chose to go forth.
He was lazy and wanted to escape the fields his brother had to plow.
His mother finally ran out of cakes, so he had nothing left at home.
chat.meaning: Mahanama walked him through the fields: plow, sow, water, reap, and it never ends. Hearing that, Anuruddha chose to go forth.
